source.title: Scaling Trends for Data Poisoning in LLMs
source.authors: Dillon Bowen; Brendan P. Murphy; Will Cai; D. Khachaturov; Adam Gleave; Kellin Pelrine

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses language-model scaling laws as background, but its experiments measure how model size relates to susceptibility to poisoned fine-tuning—not held-out pretraining loss, prediction of larger-run loss, compute-optimal allocation, or the other listed versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports scaling results for data-poisoning susceptibility. These concern a different outcome from the claim's pretraining-loss and downstream-performance versions, so the measured scaling results are recorded as none-version findings. The paper also cites prior scaling-law results; those cited results are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study measures how susceptibility to poisoned fine-tuning (learned harmfulness/bias/backdoor score) varies with log parameter count across 24 open-weight models. It measures no pretraining loss, extrapolation, compute allocation, architecture effect, or downstream task performance. Kaplan et al. is cited only as background and as a possible explanation (sample efficiency). The poisoning behaviour is also induced on purpose by the fine-tuning data. None of its results bear on any version. The record's 'discusses' overstates the engagement: the claim appears only in related work and in one speculative explanation.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that larger LLMs are generally more susceptible to data poisoning, with Gemma-2 a likely inverse-scaling exception, and that GPT models remain vulnerable despite moderation. They find no strong evidence that the trend diminishes at lower poisoning rates, though tested rates were ≥0.5%.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses poisoned-data fine-tuning and measures learned harmful or undesirable behavior; it does not reproduce a pretraining-loss scaling-law method.
record.method_sensitivity: The measured susceptibility trends vary by model series, poisoning dataset, fine-tuning epoch, and—in exploratory analyses—poisoning rate. Gemma-2 is reported as an exception to the general trend.

fits_no_version.finding: Aggregate coefficients on log parameters for learned overall score are positive at all epochs. They are significant for Harmful QA at all epochs and for Sentiment Steering at epochs 4-5, and not significant for Code Backdoor.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger fine-tuned LLMs learn harmful behaviour from poisoned fine-tuning data more readily, varying by threat model and epoch.

fits_no_version.finding: Gemma-2 posterior slopes are mostly negative, with high P(inverse scaling) for Harmful QA and Sentiment Steering; Code Backdoor is mixed.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The direction of size-vs-poisoning-susceptibility scaling can differ by model series.

fits_no_version.finding: Scale × poisoning-rate interactions are mixed. They are positive at epoch 1 for Harmful QA and Sentiment Steering, vanish for Harmful QA later, reverse for Sentiment Steering in epochs 3-5, and are never significant for Code Backdoor.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Whether size-related poisoning susceptibility depends on poisoning rate varies by task and epoch (exploratory; rates ≥0.5%).

record.problems: The study does not measure the claim's pretraining-loss outcomes. For its own poisoning-susceptibility results, it uses LoRA rather than full fine-tuning, tests poisoning rates no lower than 0.5%, and describes the poisoning-rate interaction analysis as exploratory. The Code Backdoor scale coefficients are not statistically significant at epoch 5; the authors also flag the Gemma-2 result as needing further investigation.
record.rows_left_out: none; included the reported aggregate parameter-scaling regressions (Table 2), Gemma-2 posterior trend estimates (Table 3), and scale-by-poisoning-rate interaction regressions (Table 7).

untested.parts: Pretraining loss vs parameters/tokens/compute not measured.
No extrapolation from small to large runs.
No architecture-shape comparisons at fixed size.
Fine-tuning is used, but no fine-tuning loss power law is fit; the outcome is poisoning susceptibility on a log-linear regression.
No downstream capability benchmark scaling reported.
No fitted loss exponents or allocation comparisons.

record.verdict_notes: The rows are accurately transcribed from Tables 2, 3 and 7 and correctly linked to 'none'. The Table 2 caption says standard errors were clustered by model series, while the text says by model. The GPT frontier-model results (Figure 2) are not rows, but they are irrelevant to the claim. I changed the relation to cites_only because scaling laws appear only as background and a speculative explanation. Peer-review venue as recorded was not verifiable from the text.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute.
Extrapolation from small pretraining runs to much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and its trend with compute.
Effects of architecture details on loss at fixed parameter count.
Power-law behavior in other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
Predictability of downstream task performance from scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of loss-law exponents or compute-optimal allocation on setup and fitting choices.
